threads.thread_goal: Align on scope, objectives, and initial roles for the internship programme.

messages.text:
Kicking off the Inclusive Hospitality Internship Programme Design channel. The aim is to design and pilot an internship scheme in hotels for students from diverse backgrounds, aligned with education and labour rules and grounded in social research.

I suggest we use this thread to confirm the objective for the pilot and what success will look like, and to agree on which hotels or hotel profiles we will approach first.

From the project pack, T1 and T7 are our first anchors, and A1 will be the key input once available.

Could each of you briefly react to this proposed focus for the pilot: a small cohort of students placed in 2–3 hotels, with clear safeguards and simple evaluation tools, within the next 21 days?

Thanks for starting this. From my side on T1, I can run a rapid needs assessment focusing on three groups: students, hotel staff, and education staff.

For the pilot objective, I would phrase success as: we test whether a short internship in hospitality can be organised in a way that is inclusive, does not disrupt hotel operations, and is understandable for non-specialists.

Once I have initial findings for A1, we can refine the success criteria with real barriers and opportunities. I can start short interviews and a simple survey this week.

From the academic side, I support the idea of a small pilot in 2–3 hotels. It will make it easier to monitor and to align with study requirements later.

For the objective, could we explicitly mention that the pilot should generate evidence we can use to argue for a more permanent scheme? That would help when we later connect A1 and the framework to institutional processes.

I am also curious how we define diverse backgrounds in practice here. That will affect recruitment and support.

Agree with a small, well-documented pilot. From the teaching side, I would like the objective to include at least an initial link to learning outcomes, even if we refine that later.

Maybe we can say that success includes students reporting that they understand how the internship connects to their studies, and hotel staff feeling that expectations are clear.

On hotel types, I do not have strong preferences yet, but I would avoid very small family-run places for the first round, as they may not have capacity for structured supervision.

From a communications angle, it will help if our objective is simple enough to explain in a short paragraph.

I like the idea that the pilot tests whether inclusive internships in hotels are feasible, fair to students, and workable for hotels. That gives us three pillars we can later translate into key messages and, eventually, into A6.

On hotel profiles, mid-range city hotels might be easier to explain to the public than very high-end or very niche places.

From the hotel floor, I would suggest we start with hotels that already take trainees or seasonal staff. They usually have some routines we can adapt.

For the pilot, I would be careful with very busy airport hotels or peak season in tourist areas. It is harder to give attention to interns then.

Maybe we can say we focus on medium-sized hotels in the city, with reception and housekeeping teams that can host one or two interns each.

On the definition of diverse backgrounds, I propose we keep it broad but concrete: students who are first in their family to attend higher education, students with migration backgrounds, and students with disabilities or long-term health conditions.

We will need to check with student support services and legal colleagues that our wording is consistent with existing categories and does not create new barriers.

For the pilot objective, I hear three elements: feasibility for hotels, fairness and support for students, and generation of evidence for a more permanent scheme.

I can integrate that definition of diverse backgrounds into the interview guide for T1, so that A1 reflects the experiences of those groups.

For success criteria, I suggest we also include at least one simple indicator we can measure, such as the share of interns who would recommend the experience to a peer, and the share of hotel staff who say they would host an intern again.

These can later feed into the monitoring plan in A5.

Those indicators sound workable. We can also add a short reflection question for students about how the internship affected their understanding of hospitality work and their own study path.

That will help us later when we map activities to learning outcomes.

On the hotel side, I agree with focusing on medium-sized city hotels that already have some experience with trainees. It will also make it easier to find clear examples for stories later.

For the objective statement, how about something like: The pilot will test a small-scale, inclusive internship model in 2–3 medium-sized city hotels, checking whether it works for students from diverse backgrounds and for hotel operations, and generating evidence for a longer-term scheme.

If that works for you, I can later turn it into a short public-friendly version when we work on T6.

The wording about medium-sized city hotels fits what I had in mind. In those places, supervisors usually know the team well and can spot if an intern needs extra support.

We should just be clear that interns will not be left alone at reception or in other sensitive spots, especially at night.

The proposed objective statement works for me. It is specific enough for planning and still flexible.

On success criteria, could we add that all core documents (framework, handbook, evaluation tools) should be understandable to non-specialists? That is in the project constraints and will matter for students and hotel staff.

Agree, clarity of documents should be part of success. We can later work with T8 to ensure that.

Let me try to summarise what I hear so far, and you can correct me if needed before we lock it in.

Draft summary for confirmation:

Objective for the pilot: Test a small-scale, inclusive internship model in 2–3 medium-sized city hotels that already host trainees, focusing on students from diverse backgrounds (first-generation, migration backgrounds, disabilities or long-term health conditions). The pilot will check whether the model is workable for hotel operations, fair and supportive for students, and generates evidence for a longer-term scheme.

Success criteria: (1) At least one intern placed in each pilot hotel with clear safeguards; (2) Most interns and hotel staff report they would recommend the experience; (3) Hotels report no major disruption to operations; (4) Core documents (framework, handbook, evaluation tools) are understandable to non-specialists.

If there are no strong objections, I suggest we confirm this as D1.

This summary works for me. It gives me enough direction to shape A1 and later the evaluation questions.

No changes from my side.

Looks good to me as well. The mention of evidence for a longer-term scheme is particularly helpful for the academic alignment later.

Happy to go ahead with this objective and success criteria.

I am on board with this wording. It is also something we can translate into clear public messages later without much rework.

On hotels, can we also confirm that we are not including hostels or short-stay apartments in this first round, just to keep the scope tight?

I would keep it to proper hotels for now. Hostels and apartments often have different routines and fewer staff on duty, which might make supervision harder.

Medium-sized city hotels with reception and housekeeping teams feel like the right starting point.

Agreed. For D2, I propose we define the pilot hotel profile as: medium-sized city hotels (not hostels or apartments) that already host trainees or seasonal staff, with both reception and housekeeping teams.

If you all agree, I will use this profile for T7 when mapping and approaching potential partners.

The hotel profile as you described it works for me. It should give us enough variation while keeping the context manageable.

No objections to confirming this for the pilot.
Fine by me as well. I will reflect that profile in the stakeholder list for T1 so that A1 captures views from similar hotels.

threads.thread_goal: Co-create the internship framework and ensure policy and academic alignment.

messages.text:
Starting this thread to share a first outline for the internship programme framework and policy brief under T2.

Based on our agreed pilot objective, I drafted a simple structure for A2:

1. Purpose and objectives (linking to inclusion and feasibility)
2. Eligibility and target groups
3. Roles and responsibilities (students, hotels, university)
4. Safeguards and support measures
5. Duration and workload
6. Monitoring and feedback

Before I go into more detail, I would like your views on this structure and any gaps you see, especially regarding academic alignment and practical hotel operations.

Thanks for sharing the outline. From the teaching side, I would suggest we make the link to academic requirements more explicit, perhaps as a separate section or a subsection under roles and responsibilities.

For T9, I will need a clear place in A2 where we can reference learning outcomes, credit or recognition options, and how supervisors provide feedback that can be used in assessment.

Otherwise, the structure looks workable to me.

I agree with the overall structure. To keep A2 readable for non-specialists, we might want to limit the number of sub-sections and use clear headings.

On safeguards, I would like to see explicit mention of supervision ratios, clear contact points for students if issues arise, and a short note on data protection in relation to monitoring.

We can later mirror this in the training outlines in A4 so that everyone hears the same messages.

From the research side, I would suggest that the monitoring and feedback section in A2 briefly references the indicators we discussed and the use of simple surveys.

We do not need full detail here, but a short description of how feedback will be collected and used will help when we develop A5.

Also, it might be useful to mention that the framework will be reviewed after the pilot, based on evidence from A1 and the evaluation.

Looking at the outline, I would add something under roles and responsibilities about what hotel supervisors are expected to do day to day.

For example, who shows the intern the emergency exits, who explains how to handle guest complaints, and who checks that tasks are safe and realistic.

This will also need to match what we put later in the operational handbook.

From a communications perspective, the structure is clear. When we get to T6 and T8, it will help if each section of A2 has one or two key messages that we can translate into plain language.

I would also suggest a short introductory paragraph that explains in simple terms what the programme is and who it is for, before we go into the numbered sections.

Good point on academic alignment. I can add a dedicated section 7: Academic alignment and recognition, where we reference the mapping work under T9 and any credit arrangements.

On safeguards, I will expand section 4 to include supervision ratios, contact points, and a short note on data protection, as suggested.

That addition of section 7 works for me. Once you have a draft of that part, I can propose concrete wording on learning outcomes and recognition options.

We should keep the language simple enough that students can understand what they gain from participating.

On hotel supervisors, I will make sure the roles and responsibilities section clearly states who is responsible for onboarding, daily guidance, and safety checks.

We can then ensure that A3 and the checklists in A7 are consistent with that description.

Once you have a first full draft of A2, I am happy to review it with a focus on clarity and on how it will be perceived by students and academic committees.

For the structure decision, I think we are close. Perhaps you can summarise the final list of sections so we can confirm it formally.

Here is the updated structure for A2 based on your feedback:

1. Introduction and purpose
2. Objectives of the internship programme
3. Eligibility and target groups
4. Safeguards and support (including supervision, contact points, data protection)
5. Roles and responsibilities (students, hotels, university, supervisors)
6. Duration, workload, and scheduling
7. Monitoring, feedback, and use of data
8. Academic alignment and recognition

If you are comfortable with this, we can treat it as the agreed framework structure for D3.

This structure looks solid to me. It gives us a clear home for the academic mapping and for the safeguards.

I support confirming this as the framework structure.

Agreed from my side as well. The order flows logically for readers who are not familiar with policy documents.

We can now start drafting the content under each section.

I am fine with this structure. It will also make it easier to reference specific sections when we design the evaluation tools in A5.

No changes from my side.

On mapping internship activities to academic requirements for D4, I propose the following approach:

- We define 3–4 core learning outcomes related to hospitality skills, teamwork, and inclusion.
- For each outcome, we list typical intern tasks (for example, supporting check-in under supervision, observing complaint handling, assisting with breakfast service) and link them in a simple table in T9.
- We describe in A4 how supervisors and students will reflect on these outcomes during and after the internship.

If this approach sounds reasonable, we can treat it as our decision on how to map activities to academic requirements.

I like this approach. A concise table in T9 will be easy to share with curriculum committees, and linking it to reflection activities in A4 will make the learning more visible for students.

I support using this as our agreed method for mapping activities to academic requirements.

Works for me as well. It is simple enough to implement and explain in the policy brief.

I will reference this approach in the academic alignment section of A2 so that T9 and A4 are clearly connected to the framework.

threads.thread_goal: Define practical hotel operations, intern tasks, and risk mitigation.

messages.text:
Starting this thread with a first rough list of tasks and routines that interns could realistically do in hotels, based on my experience and the needs of T3 and T11.

Possible intern tasks under supervision:
- Support at reception with simple check-in steps (for example, greeting guests, confirming bookings already in the system)
- Help with preparing breakfast area (setting tables, refilling buffet, basic cleaning)
- Assist housekeeping with non-heavy tasks (restocking amenities, checking rooms for forgotten items)
- Help with simple back-office tasks (sorting documents, preparing welcome folders)

I have not yet detailed the risks and mitigation steps. Please react to this list: what should we add, remove, or clarify before we move towards A3 and A7?

Thanks for putting this list together. From a research and inclusion angle, I would suggest we avoid tasks that involve handling cash or being solely responsible for guest complaints, at least in the pilot.

We should also think about accessibility: for example, making sure that tasks do not require lifting heavy items or standing for very long periods without breaks, so that students with some physical limitations can still participate.

These points can later be reflected in the risk list for T11.

The tasks you listed seem appropriate for an introductory internship. To support learning, we might also include some structured observation tasks, such as shadowing a receptionist during check-in or observing how housekeeping coordinates with front desk.

These can later be linked to learning outcomes in T9 and reflected in the training outlines in A4.

I agree with the list and with the idea of adding observation tasks. It would also be useful to specify which tasks are mandatory for all interns and which are optional, depending on the hotel and the student.

That will help us later when we map tasks to learning outcomes and when we explain expectations to students.

From a policy and compliance perspective, we should be clear that interns are not replacing regular staff and are not responsible for tasks that require formal certification or legal accountability.

In A3 and A7, we can mark tasks that are strictly supportive and always under supervision. This will also help when we explain the programme to labour authorities if needed.

For communication later, it will be important that the list of tasks sounds both realistic and safe. The examples you gave are easy to explain to the public.

When we draft A6, we can use a short description of a typical intern day based on this list, to make the programme more concrete.

Good points. I agree that interns should not handle cash or be the main person for complaints.

I will adjust the list to focus on supportive tasks only and will note that any direct guest interaction is under supervision. I will also add a note about avoiding heavy lifting and making sure breaks are planned.

I like the idea of observation tasks. In practice, that could mean the intern stands next to the receptionist during check-in, listens to how they welcome guests, and then discusses what they noticed afterwards.

I will include a small section in the draft for A3 on observation and reflection moments.

On risks for T11, here are some that come to mind:

- Interns left unsupervised at reception
- Interns asked to lift heavy luggage
- Confusion about working hours and breaks
- Exposure to aggressive guest behaviour without support

For each of these, we can define simple mitigation steps, such as clear rules on supervision, a list of tasks that are off-limits, and a short briefing on how to escalate difficult situations.

These risks match what I see on the floor. I can expand the list to reach at least eight items for T11 and write short, practical mitigation steps in simple language.

I will also make sure that the onboarding checklist in A7 includes a safety walk-through and a clear explanation of who the intern can call if something feels wrong.

Once you have the risk list and mitigation steps drafted, I can review them with an eye on inclusion and student wellbeing.

We should also ensure that the same points appear in the student training outline in A4 so that students know what to expect and what is not acceptable.

To move towards a decision on the task list for D5, could you, 19278, share a cleaned-up version of the tasks, grouped by area (reception, housekeeping, breakfast, back-office) and clearly marked as supportive and supervised?

Then we can quickly confirm that as the allowed task list for the pilot.

Here is a cleaned-up proposal for allowed tasks for the pilot:

Reception (always supervised):
- Greeting guests and directing them to the receptionist
- Checking basic booking details already in the system
- Preparing key cards and welcome materials

Breakfast area:
- Setting and clearing tables
- Refilling buffet items that are not hot or heavy
- Wiping surfaces and keeping the area tidy

Housekeeping:
- Restocking amenities (soap, towels, tea)
- Checking rooms for forgotten items after check-out
- Reporting maintenance issues to supervisors

Back-office:
- Preparing welcome folders and information packs
- Sorting non-confidential documents

All tasks are supportive and under supervision. No cash handling, no being alone at reception, no heavy lifting.

If this looks acceptable, we can use it as the base for A3 and A7.

This list looks balanced and consistent with the risks we discussed. It should also be easy to explain to students and hotel staff.

I support confirming this as the allowed task list for the pilot.

Agreed from my side. The grouping by area will also help when we design reflection activities and link tasks to learning outcomes.

No further changes needed.

Thanks for the clear list. We will treat this as the agreed task set for D5.

On D6, for risk mitigation and onboarding, I propose we define three standard steps for all pilot hotels:

1. A structured first-day onboarding using A7, including safety tour and role explanation.
2. A named supervisor for each intern, with a short daily check-in.
3. A simple incident and feedback log, linked to the monitoring plan in A5.

If you agree, we can confirm these as the core mitigation and onboarding measures.

These three steps cover the main needs I see from the student side. The daily check-in and the incident log will also give us useful qualitative information for the evaluation.

I support confirming them as the standard mitigation and onboarding measures.

Agreed. The incident and feedback log will be a valuable input for A5 and for the pilot summary later.

No objections from my side.

threads.thread_goal: Finalize evaluation tools and data collection approach for the pilot.

messages.text:
Starting this thread to share a first draft of the evaluation plan and survey templates under T4.

For A5, I propose we focus on three main evaluation questions:

1. Is the internship feasible for hotels without major disruption?
2. Is the internship fair and supportive for students from diverse backgrounds?
3. Does the internship generate useful evidence for a longer-term scheme?

I have drafted a short pre- and post-internship survey for students and a short survey for hotel supervisors, plus an interview guide for a few follow-up conversations. I would like your feedback on indicators, question wording, and practicalities before we finalise and move to T10.

The three evaluation questions align well with our agreed objectives.

On indicators, I would suggest we include:
- Student satisfaction with supervision and clarity of tasks
- Student perception of how the internship connects to their studies
- Hotel perception of workload and disruption

For the interview guide, it would be good to have at least one open question about inclusion, for example asking whether students felt they could bring their full selves to the workplace.

From the academic side, I would add an indicator on perceived learning: for example, asking students to rate how much they feel they have developed specific skills linked to our learning outcomes.

We should also keep the surveys short enough that students and hotel staff are willing to complete them, ideally no more than 10 questions each.

From a policy perspective, it would be useful to include one or two items that help us argue for scaling, such as whether hotels would host interns again and whether students would recommend the programme.

We should also make sure that any questions about health or background are phrased carefully and in line with data protection rules. I can check the draft against our institutional guidance once you share it.

On wording, I would recommend we avoid jargon and keep questions very straightforward, especially for hotel staff who may be filling this in quickly.

If you share the draft text, I can help simplify the language so that it is consistent with what we will later use in A6 and in any public-facing summaries.

From the hotel floor, I would keep the supervisor survey very short, maybe 5–7 questions, and mostly multiple choice.

Supervisors often fill these things in between tasks, so if it is too long, it might not get done.

Thanks for the suggestions. I will make sure the indicators you mentioned are clearly reflected in the survey items.

On inclusion, I will add an open question inviting students to share whether they felt welcomed and supported, and whether any aspect of their background made the experience easier or harder.

Good point on perceived learning. I will add a short list of skills linked to our learning outcomes and ask students to rate their development on a simple scale.

I will also keep an eye on total length and aim for around 8–10 questions per survey, as you suggested.

I will include items on willingness to host interns again and willingness to recommend the programme, both for students and hotels.

For sensitive questions, I will keep them optional and phrase them in a way that focuses on experience rather than labels. Once the draft is ready, I will share it so you can check it against institutional guidance.

I will send you the draft questions shortly so you can help simplify the wording.

We should also make sure that the terms we use in the surveys match those in A2 and A3, to avoid confusion.

Happy to help. Once I see the draft, I will focus on making the questions short, clear, and consistent with the rest of our materials.

We can also test the wording with one or two colleagues who are not involved in the project, as a quick clarity check.

On ethical and privacy considerations, we should clearly state in A5 that participation in surveys and interviews is voluntary, that responses are confidential, and that data will be reported in aggregate.

I can review the ethics section once you have a draft and confirm that it aligns with our usual research standards.

I will add a dedicated section on ethics and privacy in A5, covering voluntary participation, confidentiality, and data storage.

Once that is in place, I will share the document with you for review and approval.

To move towards D7, here is a summary of the indicators and tools we are converging on:

- Student pre-survey: expectations, initial confidence, any concerns.
- Student post-survey: satisfaction with supervision and tasks, perceived learning, sense of inclusion, willingness to recommend.
- Hotel supervisor survey: perceived workload and disruption, clarity of framework, willingness to host again.
- Short interview guide for a small sample of students and supervisors, focusing on inclusion and feasibility.

All tools will be short, use simple language, and include clear information on voluntary participation and confidentiality.

If you agree with this set, we can treat it as our final indicator and survey package for the pilot.

This package covers the key aspects we need to understand the pilot. I am comfortable treating it as our agreed set of indicators and tools.

Once I see the full draft of A5, I will focus on the ethics and clarity sections.

Agreed from my side as well. The willingness-to-host-again and willingness-to-recommend items will be particularly useful for policy discussions.

No further additions from me.

The tools you described sound manageable for hotel supervisors, especially if the survey is short.

I support using this set for the pilot.

threads.thread_goal: Align on communication strategy and public narrative for the programme.

messages.text:
Starting this thread to share draft key messages and a simple communication plan under T6.

For A6, I propose three core messages:

1. The programme tests a small-scale, inclusive internship model in medium-sized city hotels, focusing on students from diverse backgrounds.
2. The internships are designed to be fair to students and workable for hotels, with clear safeguards and support.
3. The pilot will generate evidence to decide whether and how to scale the programme.

Channels: internal university newsletter, direct emails to potential partner hotels, and a short web article. External media outreach only after we have first pilot results.

I would like your feedback on these messages, the choice of channels, and any risks you see before we sign off for D8.

The three messages align well with our agreed objectives and with the structure of A2.

From a policy angle, I would add a short line that the programme is aligned with existing education and labour regulations and that it does not replace regular jobs.

On channels, I agree with starting with internal and direct communication and waiting with broader media until we have pilot results.

From the research side, it would be good if we mention that the programme is evidence-informed and that we will use simple surveys and feedback tools to learn from the pilot.

This can help manage expectations and show that we are not promising more than we can deliver at this stage.

I like the clarity of the three messages. For students, we should also highlight what they can gain: practical experience in hospitality, better understanding of hotel work, and a clearer link to their studies.

We should avoid language that makes the programme sound like charity; instead, we can frame it as a structured learning opportunity that is open and supportive.

For academic audiences, it might help to mention that the internships are linked to learning outcomes and that we are exploring options for recognition or credit.

This can go into the internal newsletter and any communication with programme directors.

For hotels, I would keep the message very practical: what is expected from them, how many interns, for how long, and what support they get.

It might also help to mention that interns will not be left alone with critical tasks and that there is a clear contact person at the university.

Thanks, I will add a short line about alignment with regulations and about not replacing regular jobs.

On the evidence point, I will also mention that we are using simple surveys and feedback tools, without going into technical detail.

Good reminder on tone. I will frame the programme as a structured learning opportunity that is open and supportive, and highlight concrete benefits for students, such as practical experience and better understanding of hospitality work.

For hotels, I will keep the language focused on clarity and support, as 19278 suggested.

I will include a short note in the internal newsletter text that the internships are linked to learning outcomes and that we are exploring recognition options, referencing the mapping work in T9.

That should help bring programme directors on board.

On channels, I would add one more: a short briefing note for student support services, so they can explain the programme to students who might be interested.

We should also agree that any external media requests go through you, to avoid mixed messages.

Agreed. I will prepare a short briefing note for student support services and include a line in A6 that any external media requests should be routed through the communications contact.

This will help us keep the narrative consistent and avoid misunderstandings.

One small suggestion: when we talk about students from diverse backgrounds, we might want to give a few examples, as we did in the framework, but also stress that the programme is open and does not require students to disclose anything they are not comfortable sharing.

This can help avoid any perception that we are labelling students.

Good point. I will mirror the examples from the framework and add a line that students can choose what they share and that support is available regardless.

This should make the messaging more sensitive and reassuring.

To move towards D8, here is a consolidated proposal:

Key messages:
- The pilot tests a small-scale, inclusive internship model in medium-sized city hotels for students from diverse backgrounds, aligned with existing education and labour rules.
- Internships are structured, supervised, and designed to be fair to students and workable for hotels, without replacing regular jobs.
- The pilot uses simple surveys and feedback tools to learn what works and to decide whether and how to scale the programme.
- Students gain practical hospitality experience linked to their studies, and hotels receive clear support and contact points.

Channels for launch:
- Internal university newsletter (students and staff)
- Direct emails to potential partner hotels
- Briefing note for student support services
- Short web article on the university site

External media outreach only after pilot results are available, and any media requests during the pilot go through the communications contact.

If you are comfortable with this, we can treat it as our agreed communication package.

This summary captures the main points we need to communicate and is consistent with the framework.

I support treating it as our agreed communication package for the pilot.

Agreed from my side. The messages are clear for students and staff, and the channels seem appropriate for this stage.

No further changes needed.

The way you describe expectations and support for hotels feels realistic. I think hotel managers will appreciate the clarity.

I support using this package for outreach.

Looks good to me as well. The reference to simple surveys and feedback tools sets the right expectations.

Happy to go ahead with this.
